I'm Kalyani, and last spring I nearly walked out of the research lab in Pune with a resignation letter and a speech. I'd found that the trial summary going to the funder left out two failed runs. I was furious. I wanted to email the whole department and slam the door.
Instead I called Tejas sir, who had supervised my thesis. He listened for twenty minutes without interrupting. Then he said, "Don't resign today. Write down exactly what's missing, with dates. Take it to the research integrity office. A dramatic exit feels brave, but it lets them bury the problem with you gone."
I trusted him. He'd seen three labs. But I also said, "Sir, if they ask me to sign that summary, I won't." He nodded. "Good. That's the line. Keep it."
Looking back, he helped me do the right thing, not just the safe thing.

qa.a: Two failed runs.

qa.a: Kalyani was furious and wanted to make a dramatic exit, emailing the whole department and resigning.

Mentor's note, Friday evening.
Jahnavi came to see me after her team lead asked her to backdate three client approval emails for the tax audit. She was shaking and had her resignation typed on her phone. She said, "I'll just leave. Let them deal with it."
I understand the instinct. I asked her to wait one day. We went through the steps together: save the lead's message, write down what was asked and when, and raise it with the compliance officer on Monday morning. I told her resigning in anger could leave her with no reference and no record of what happened.
She asked, "And if compliance says do it anyway?" I said then she refuses to backdate, whatever the cost, and I would support her in finding a new job. Some lines are not about process.
She deleted the typed resignation before leaving. We meet again Monday at 5.
Zainab

"Sure, Abhinav. Sit."
He had practised this in the mirror. His palms were still damp. "I've been here two years. I looked at the salary survey from the industry association, and for data engineers with my experience in Bengaluru, the range is above where I am."

Last October I finally made a list. What editors at my level were paid, from two job portals and three friends. What I'd done: the two books I rescued from deadline disasters, the new freelancer system I set up.
I booked a meeting with Naveen, the publisher. My voice wobbled at the start. But I said it: "I'd like my pay reviewed, and here's why."
He was quiet for a while. Then he said, "Not this quarter. Maybe in April."
It stung. But he didn't say no because I was greedy. He said no because of money. In April, I asked again. That time, he said yes.

It was 11 p.m., two hours before the app launch, the office pantry littered with pizza boxes, when Tanuja caught Chinmay, the founder, by the coffee machine. "Can we talk about my salary review? It was due in June."
Chinmay sighed. "Tanu, right now? We're a family here. Families don't count every rupee. And honestly, a hundred people would love your job."
Her cheeks went hot. For a second she felt ungrateful, greedy, small. Then she noticed the pattern: the family line, the hundred people, the guilt, and no answer to her question.
"I love working here," she said evenly. "That's why I want it to be fair. I'm not asking tonight. Could we fix a meeting this week, and could you send me the review criteria in writing?"
Chinmay blinked. "Fine. Thursday."
She sent a short email confirming Thursday before going back to her desk.

Last year the landlord's lease arrived. Twelve pages. I asked her, "Is it okay? Just tell me where to sign."

passage:
Jomon, the contractor, sat on the bench outside Rashmi's small bakery in Pala, the renovation contract in a plastic folder. "Sign today, chechi. Tomorrow my team goes to a job in Kottayam. Then you'll wait three months."
Rashmi read slowly. On the phone he had promised new wiring, a steel counter and cleanup included. The paper said only "renovation work as discussed". There was a line about "extra charges as applicable".
"The wiring and counter aren't written here," she said.
"Arre, I told you. My word is enough."
Rashmi felt her chest tighten. She wanted the bakery ready before the Onam rush. But she remembered her neighbour's leaking roof after a contract just like this.
"Then write your word down. Each item, and what 'extra charges' means. I'll sign then."
Jomon stood. "I don't have time."
"Then I'll wait." She kept a photo of the contract and his phone promises, and called another contractor that evening.

qa.q: What did the contract say instead of listing the work?
qa.a: Only "renovation work as discussed", plus a line about "extra charges as applicable".

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when Jomon said his word was enough?
qa.a: She felt tense and torn, anxious to be ready for Onam but wary because of her neighbour's bad experience.

qa.q: How did Rashmi protect herself?
qa.a: She asked for each promised item and the extra charges in writing, refused to sign under time pressure, kept records, and found another contractor.

qa.q: How might Jomon see Rashmi's refusal?
qa.a: Jomon seems annoyed and impatient, used to people signing quickly under pressure, and walks away rather than write things down.

grounding: A contractor keeps promises verbal, leaves vague fees and pressures a same-day signing; the protagonist insists on written terms and walks away.
